newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh says Burma refugees still refuse food.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh says Burma refugees still refuse food.

text.p: Thousands of Burmese Moslem refugees living in camps in Bangladesh refused food rations for a 14th day on Monday, but officials expressed hope they would soon change their minds.
"So far we have not been able to convince the majority of them to accept their rations," one relief official said after visiting the Nayapara refugee camp in the district of Cox's Bazar.
"A small section of the camp's more than 13,000 inmates collected their rations on Sunday following a lead by comrades in the other camp at Kutupalong," the official told Reuters.
"We hope those still reluctant will change their minds soon."
There are about 21,000 of the refugees in Bangladesh, with about 13,000 at Nayapara and 8,000 in Kutupalong.

The food boycott started on July 21 as part of a protest by the Burmese Moslems, known as Rohingyas, against what they believe are attempts by the Bangladesh government to send them back home by force.
Violence over the issue left at least 20 people, including six policemen, injured at the Nayapara camp, which forced authorities to suspend the repatriation process.

Government officials and representatives of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNCHR) persuaded the refugees at Kutupalong to end their food boycott last week and some of the Nayapara inmates later collected their rations on Sunday.

The refugees are the remnants of some 250,000 Rohingyas who crossed into southeastern Bangladesh in early 1992 from western Burma's Moslem-majority Arakan province to escape alleged persecution by Burma's military junta.
"They are using the same pretext (persecution) now to support their demand for not going back to Burma," one government official in Chittagong said.

"While we have repeatedly reaffirmed to the refugees and the UNHCR that no one would be forced back to Burma we remain also firm in our position that Bangladesh cannot give permanent residence to the Rohingyas," he said.
Witnesses said refugees at Nayapara on Monday shouted abuse at policemen guarding the camp and threatened even tougher action against repatriation bids.
"The situation at Nayapara was still very tense," one witness said.
